findings.description: storage_encrypted is explicitly set to false, so the RDS volume, snapshots and automated backups store the database contents unencrypted. Any compromise of the underlying storage or a shared snapshot exposes all data in cleartext.

publicly_accessible = true assigns the MySQL instance a public endpoint reachable from the internet (the endpoint is also exported as an output), moving the database from a private VPC-only asset to an internet-facing attack surface protected only by a password.

The master user is the well-known default 'admin', which removes any need for an attacker to guess the account name when brute-forcing the internet-exposed endpoint. Combined with publicly_accessible = true this materially lowers the bar for credential attacks.

The user_data script interpolates var.password and the DB username into /var/www/inc/dbinfo.inc. EC2 user data is retrievable in cleartext from the instance metadata service by any process or SSRF-capable application on the host, and is visible in the Terraform state and EC2 console, leaking the database master password.

No metadata_options block is specified, so IMDSv1 (token-less) remains enabled. Because the instance runs a PHP application that accepts user input and carries a wildcard IAM role plus a password in user data, a single SSRF or RCE yields both the AWS credentials and the DB password via a simple HTTP GET to 169.254.169.254.
No root_block_device / ebs_block_device encryption is configured, so the instance's root volume (which holds the plaintext dbinfo.inc credentials file) is stored unencrypted.

The instance role grants s3:*, ec2:* and rds:* on Resource "*". This violates least privilege and provides a direct privilege-escalation and lateral-movement path: ec2:* permits creating instances with other roles and modifying security groups, s3:* permits reading or deleting every bucket in the account, and rds:* permits snapshotting or deleting any database.

Egress allows all protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0 from the database security group, providing no outbound segmentation and enabling data exfiltration or command-and-control traffic from a compromised data-tier resource.

The MySQL 8.0 parameter group sets only character-set parameters and does not set require_secure_transport = 1, so clients (including the PHP mysqli_connect call, which requests no TLS) may connect to the internet-exposed instance over an unencrypted channel, exposing credentials and query data.
